h1: SEO for diagnostic labs, where the query is a test name and a price
metaTitle: SEO for Diagnostic Labs: Test and Price Pages
metaDescription: SEO for diagnostic labs in India. We build one page per test with price, prep and report time, then win the map pack for home collection searches.
answer: Diagnostic lab SEO scales on one repeatable unit: a page per test carrying price, fasting instructions, sample type and report turnaround. Those four fields answer the entire query. Around them sit package pages for full body checkups and home-collection serviceability, and above both, the map pack for `lab near me`.
takeaways: The query is `vitamin d test price` — four fields answer it, and most lab sites publish none of them. Price is not a sales conversation you defer; it is the search.
Your competitor is not the lab across the road. It's an aggregator with a page for every test in every city, and a national chain with a fifteen-year-old domain.
**Pincode pages are where diagnostic SEO dies.** 19,000 near-identical serviceability URLs is scaled content abuse, and it takes the whole domain down, not just those pages.
Full body checkup queries are comparison queries. Publish the parameter list, not the parameter count.
NABL accreditation, a named pathologist and an honest turnaround time do more for conversion than any amount of stock imagery of a centrifuge.

sections.h2: A test page is four fields long
body: Type `thyroid test price near me` and watch what the results are trying to do. Every one races to answer the same short list: what it costs, whether you need to fast, what sample they take, when the report lands. That's the entire informational payload of a diagnostic query, and it fits in a table.

Labs lose these searches for a non-technical reason: marketing treats price as something to capture a lead for. Your page says "call for pricing", the aggregator says ₹499, and the customer never sees your name again. You didn't lose on domain authority. You lost on refusing to answer.

callout.title: The unit economics of this template
callout.body: A mid-size lab runs 300–800 orderable tests. At one page each that's a content programme, not a blog. It is genuinely repeatable though — identical fields, different values — which makes it the rare case where systematic page generation is legitimate rather than spammy. The line is whether each page carries data true only of that test.

sections.h2: You're not competing with the lab across the road
body: Search any test name with `price` and look at who ranks. Health aggregators — Tata 1mg, Practo, Apollo 24|7, Healthians, Redcliffe — plus national chains like Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis and Thyrocare. Older domains, more links, and a page for every test crossed with every city. On raw domain strength you won't beat them, and an agency promising you'll outrank 1mg for `cbc test price` is selling a fantasy.

What you can win is narrower and more valuable: local intent, where proximity beats authority; your own brand plus test name, which aggregators can't own; long-tail test names their templates render badly; and the informational layer — what a test means, why it was ordered, what an out-of-range value indicates — which they template and rarely write well.

subs.h3: The price parity problem nobody wants to discuss
body: You list a test at ₹700 on your own site and ₹499 on the aggregator, because the aggregator demanded the discount. Then you spend money ranking the page quoting the higher number — teaching your own customer to book through a channel that charges you commission, using your search visibility to do it.

SEO can't fix a pricing structure that punishes direct booking. Either match the direct price, or give the direct booker something the aggregator can't: a preferred collection slot, a free repeat within seven days, a doctor call-back on abnormal results. Decide before you commission the content.

sections.h2: Home collection, and the pincode-page trap
body: Home collection is the growth channel, and `blood test at home` plus a locality name is the query. It's also where diagnostic sites most reliably destroy themselves, because someone works out that India has around 19,000 pincodes and generates a page for each.

Those pages are identical except for a variable. Google classifies that as scaled content abuse, and the damage isn't confined to the thin pages — it drags the domain. We've set out where [programmatic SEO crosses the line](/journal/programmatic-seo-and-the-scaled-content-line) in detail; the test is simple. Does this page carry a fact true only of this location?
numbered: **With real per-area data, build the page.** Which lab processes that area, the actual collection slot windows, the earliest morning slot, report time from that pincode, phlebotomist coverage.
**Without it, build one page and a serviceability checker.** A single strong home-collection page plus a pincode input beats 19,000 templates on both traffic and risk.

**Do build locality pages where you have a physical centre.** A collection centre in Kandivali justifies a Kandivali page with directions, hours, staff and parking. Ten centres, ten pages. Not four hundred.
**Instrument the WhatsApp path.** Plenty of home-collection bookings arrive there. Tag the links with URL parameters or you'll conclude SEO isn't working while it quietly is.

callout.title: The tell in an agency proposal
callout.body: If a proposal promises "20,000 location pages in month one", read it as a plan to put your domain at risk for a traffic spike that reverses. Ask what unique data goes on each page. If the answer is the pincode itself, that's your answer.

sections.h2: Full body checkups are a comparison query, not a product
body: `full body checkup price`, `best full body checkup package`, `which health checkup should I do at 40` — among the highest-volume commercial searches in Indian diagnostics, and all comparison searches. The person has three tabs open. Be the page that makes comparison easy rather than the one hiding the details.

That means publishing the full parameter list, not the number. "92 parameters" is a marketing artefact; clinicians will tell you a longer panel isn't automatically a better checkup, and a reader told that once trusts the lab that said it. List what's included, group it by system, and mark what each group screens for.
bullets: **A comparison table across your own packages** — basic, advanced, cardiac, diabetic, women's, seniors — with parameters, price and turnaround side by side. This is the shape that wins featured snippets for `which checkup` queries.
**Age and risk guidance**, written by your pathologist. "At 30 with no family history, here's what's reasonable" is content nobody in the category publishes and everybody searches for.
**What the package doesn't cover.** The single most trust-building line on the page.
**Package pages linked to the individual test pages** they contain. That internal linking is what makes the test-page library rank, and it's the step most labs skip.

sections.h2: Accreditation, the pathologist, and the schema that's worth doing
body: Diagnostics is a trust purchase disguised as a price comparison. People compare on price, then check whether the lab is real. Give them something to find.

NABL accreditation to ISO 15189 is the recognised standard for medical testing labs in India. If you hold it, the certificate number and the accredited scope belong on the page — as a fact, not a footer logo. Same for NABH, and for registration under the Clinical Establishments Act in states that have adopted it. Name the consultant pathologist, with qualification and registration number, and let them sign the interpretation content. A named MD Pathology reviewing your test explainers beats any link-building campaign in this category.
bullets: **`MedicalTest` and lab-related types exist in schema.org** and are worth implementing for machine readability, even where Google shows no rich result for them today.
**`LocalBusiness` markup on each centre page**, with hours, address and geo, feeding the local surface.
**FAQ rich results were restricted in 2023** to well-known authoritative government and health sites. A lab may qualify; plan as though it won't, and treat any rich result as a bonus.
**Report turnaround honesty.** Promising 6 hours and delivering 30 generates one-star reviews, and reviews are a local ranking input. Your SEO and your operations share a number here.

sections.h2: What this costs, and what we actually guarantee
body: A single collection centre or small standalone lab sits at ₹40,000/mo with us. A multi-centre lab with a 400-test library, package pages and a home-collection programme is ₹75,000/mo and up — a content system, a set of local listings and a real architecture problem. All ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, every asset yours. [Local SEO costs](/cost/local-seo-cost) breaks the local side down further.

Measure four things, not traffic: bookings completed on the site, calls from the Google profile, WhatsApp enquiries tagged at source, and walk-ins attributed with a code at reception. Diagnostics has an unusually clean line from search to revenue, so a report leading with sessions has no excuse.

We don't guarantee a ranking position. Nobody controls Google's index, and you'd be suspicious of a lab that guaranteed a result before running the sample. We freeze your trailing-90-day count of qualified enquiries from organic search on day one and beat it within 90 days — or we keep working free until we do. Three clients a month is why we can carry that. Here's [how we run SEO](/seo).

callout.title: The realistic curve
callout.body: Google Business Profile and review work on collection centres often shows movement in four to eight weeks. Test-page libraries take three to six months to compound, because the pages need internal links from package pages and informational content before they carry weight. Anyone promising aggregator-beating rankings in month one is describing a different, easier problem than yours.

faqs.q: Should a diagnostic lab publish test prices on its website?
faqs.a: Yes. `test name + price` is the query, and the page that answers it captures the click. Withholding the price sends the searcher to an aggregator that publishes theirs, and you pay a commission on the booking you'd otherwise have owned. Publish the price with the fasting instructions and the report time.

faqs.q: Can a local lab outrank 1mg or Dr Lal PathLabs for test price searches?
faqs.a: For national head terms, realistically no — those domains have a decade of authority and a page per test per city. What you can win is local intent, near-me and locality searches, your own brand plus test name, long-tail test names their templates handle badly, and the interpretation content they template poorly.

faqs.q: Are pincode pages a good idea for home collection SEO?
faqs.a: Only where each page carries something true of that area — the processing lab, real collection slot windows, report timing, coverage. Generating thousands of near-identical pincode URLs is scaled content abuse and Google can suppress the whole domain for it. One strong page plus a serviceability checker is safer and usually performs better.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to work for a diagnostic centre?
faqs.a: Local profile and review work often moves in four to eight weeks, because the map pack is the fastest-responding surface in search. A test-page library takes three to six months to compound, since those pages need internal links from package and informational content before they rank against aggregators.

Not as a direct ranking factor. It helps in the two places that matter more: conversion, because people checking whether a lab is genuine look for it, and credibility signals for health content, where verifiable accreditation and a named pathologist support the expertise Google's raters are asked to assess.

faqs.q: What should a full body checkup page include?
faqs.a: The complete parameter list grouped by body system, not just the parameter count. Price, fasting requirements, report turnaround, what the package does not cover, and a comparison table against your other packages. Age and risk guidance written by your pathologist is the part nobody else publishes.
